slides.say: By now we already know that the questions on this exam are special. They give an advantage to students who think in a more creative way.
In the previous lessons we learned three super-methods, plugging in the answers, plugging in numbers, and estimating. They help us solve a large part of the exam questions faster and more easily.

Here and there, there are also questions we call insight questions. To solve them, you need one creative idea, and that idea doesn't repeat. It belongs to that one question. What works in one question won't work in another.

slides: These questions are rarer. Most questions fit our super-methods. But they're on the exam, so we'll practice them too.

slides.say: So how do we find the idea? Before you start calculating, stop for a few seconds and look at the question. Ask yourself, what's special here?
Look for numbers that repeat, for something that's exactly double or half of something else, for parts that two things share, or for something in the story that doesn't change.
at: or for something in the story

slides.say: Why does it work? Because the people who write the exam choose the numbers on purpose. When a question looks long, there's often a short way hidden in its numbers, and the exam rewards the student who spots it.
Here's a short example. Forty-eight plus seventy-three plus ninety-six, minus, the bracket forty-six plus seventy-one plus ninety-four. What is it?

One way is to calculate. Forty-eight plus seventy-three is a hundred twenty-one, plus ninety-six is two hundred seventeen. Forty-six plus seventy-one is a hundred seventeen, plus ninety-four is two hundred eleven. Two hundred seventeen minus two hundred eleven is six. It works, but it takes time, and it's easy to slip.
at: plus ninety-six is two hundred seventeen

slides.say: Now let's look before we calculate. Every number in the first bracket has a partner in the second bracket that's a little smaller. Forty-eight and forty-six, seventy-three and seventy-one, ninety-six and ninety-four.
Each partner is smaller by two. There are three pairs, so the whole difference is two plus two plus two, six. No big sums at all.
at: Each partner is smaller by two

slides: Why is that allowed? When we take away a sum, we take away each of its numbers. So we can match each number with its partner, in any order we like.

slides.say: So when do we look for an insight? When the calculation looks long or messy, and the numbers look chosen on purpose. When they repeat, when one is double another, or when two things share parts. That's the sign to stop and look before you calculate.
And the trap is the opposite. Starting to calculate right away, before you even looked at the question.
at: And the trap is the opposite

slides: How do we get ready for these questions? Simply by practicing as many of them as we can. That opens your mind, and it will help you on the exam. Let's see a few sample questions like this. [pause] Okay. I'll see you in the next video.
